issues.legal_issue: A High Court may correct an apparent error of law in concurrent revenue decisions classifying an occupant as a trespasser when the facts do not establish the statutory conditions for trespass.
material_facts: The landowner sued for possession, and the revenue appellate authority and Board of Revenue found the occupant to be a trespasser.
Documents in the record showed that the landowner had let the land to the occupant for rent.
The landowner did not allege that the occupant prevented him from occupying land duly let to him.
The record did not establish that the occupant took or retained possession without authority.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in exercising its writ jurisdiction to correct the apparent error of law and quash the revenue authorities’ decisions.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court may correct an apparent error of law in revenue decisions. Section 5(44) of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 defines a trespasser as a person who takes or retains possession without authority or prevents another person from occupying land duly let to that person. The evidence did not establish either condition. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_review_of_concurrent_revenue_decisions and land_was_leased_to_occupant and not occupant_possession_was_proven_unauthorized and not claimant_was_prevented_from_occupying_duly_leased_land

predicates.constitutional_writ_review_of_concurrent: A party sought constitutional writ review of concurrent revenue decisions classifying an occupant as a trespasser.
predicates.land_was_leased_to_occupant: The claimant had let the land to the occupant.
predicates.occupant_possession_was_proven_unauthori: The record established that the occupant took or retained possession without authority.
predicates.claimant_was_prevented_from_occupying_du: The occupant prevented the claimant from occupying land duly let to the claimant.

issues.definition: When a party seeks writ review of concurrent revenue decisions, the land was leased to the occupant, and neither unauthorized possession nor prevention of the claimant’s occupation is established, the decisions may be quashed for apparent legal error.

issues.legal_issue: An alternative claim for ejectment cannot be entertained when the necessary facts for that claim have neither been adequately pleaded nor proved.
material_facts: The possession suit was framed alternatively under the statutory ejectment provision.
The suit was not decreed on that alternative basis.
The necessary averments and proof of facts for the alternative claim were absent.
issues.conclusion: The alternative ejectment claim could not be entertained.
issues.legal_principle: Section 180 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 applies to ejectment suits concerning specified categories of tenants, including Khudkasht or Ghair-Khatedar tenants and sub-tenants. Section 5(23) defines Khudkasht, and the Act determines the relevant tenant and sub-tenant categories. A claim under section 180 requires the necessary averments and proof of facts; the judgment relies on no earlier cases.

predicates.tenancy_suit_includes_alternative_ejectm: A party included an alternative ejectment claim in a tenancy suit.
predicates.necessary_ejectment_category_facts_plead: The claimant pleaded the facts needed to place the occupant or land within a category eligible for the claimed ejectment remedy.
predicates.necessary_ejectment_category_facts_prove: The claimant proved the facts needed to place the occupant or land within a category eligible for the claimed ejectment remedy.

issues.definition: If a tenancy suit includes an alternative ejectment claim but the necessary category facts were neither pleaded nor proved, the alternative claim cannot be entertained.
